title: Do Emergent Misalignment Models Share a Circuit?

paper.title: Do Emergent Misalignment Models Share a Circuit?
paper.abstract:
Abstract Fine-tuning language models on narrowly defined harmful tasks can induce
emergent misalignment (EM) across unrelated domains. While prior work
has identified shared misalignment-associated representations across
independently fine-tuned models, it remains unclear whether these
models rely on common computational components. We investigate this
question using three LoRA fine-tunes of Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct trained
on harmful medical advice, risky financial advice, and extreme-sports
recommendations. Using direction-based activation tracing, we identify
three attention-head locations shared among the five highest-ranked
heads of all three organisms. Replacing each organism’s five selected
head contributions with Base contributions reduces free-generation EM from 38.9% to
22.9% for medical, 50.7% to 12.5% for finance, and 41.7% to
11.1% for sports, outperforming layer-matched random interventions
without reducing judged coherence. Cross-organism activation transfer
further shows that the shared heads exhibit partially interchangeable
effects on fixed-response preference. These findings provide evidence
that representational convergence in EM extends to shared, causally
relevant attention-head components within a common model architecture.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Fine-tuning language models on narrowly defined tasks can induce behavioral changes that extend beyond the training domain. A striking example is emergent misalignment (EM), in which models fine-tuned on harmful examples from a specific domain exhibit misaligned behavior in otherwise unrelated contexts [ 2 ] . This phenomenon has been studied using model organisms trained on harmful medical advice, risky financial advice, and extreme-sports recommendations [ 7 ] . Although the fine-tuning data targets a restricted set of behaviors, the resulting misalignment can generalize across substantially different prompts. This raises a mechanistic question: how does narrow-domain fine-tuning produce such broad changes in behavior? Recent work has begun to address this question by examining the internal representations associated with emergent misalignment. In particular, similar misalignment-associated activation directions have been identified across independently fine-tuned models, and interventions along these directions have been shown to influence model behavior [ 6 ] . These findings suggest that different EM fine-tunes may share a common representational structure. However, whether this convergence extends to the underlying computational mechanisms remains an open question. In particular, it is unclear whether independently fine-tuned models rely on the same attention-head components to produce misaligned behavior. In this work, we investigate this distinction by examining attention-head contributions across three LoRA fine-tunes of Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, trained independently on harmful medical advice, risky financial advice, and extreme-sports recommendations. For each fine-tune, we estimate a misalignment-associated direction in the residual stream using contrasts between aligned and misaligned responses. We then trace the contribution of individual attention heads to this direction by substituting their fine-tuned outputs into the corresponding base-model computation. This direction-based approach allows us to study a behavioral property expressed over complete responses without reducing misalignment to the prediction of a particular output token [ 5 ] . By applying the same procedure across fine-tunes, we identify candidate attention heads and examine the extent to which their locations are shared. Three of the five highest-ranked head locations recur in every fine-tune. Reverting each organism’s selected five heads to Base contributions reduces generated EM relative to matched random replacements. On fixed response sequences, activations at the three shared locations also partially substitute across organisms. Together, these tests distinguish recurrent head locations from their effects on behavior and their functional correspondence across fine-tunes.

sections.heading: 2.1 Emergent Misalignment and Representational Convergence
sections.text: Emergent misalignment (EM) occurs when fine-tuning on a narrow task induces misaligned behavior beyond the training domain. Betley et al. [ 2 ] demonstrated this effect using insecure code, while Turner et al. [ 7 ] extended it to medical, financial, and extreme-sports domains and showed that EM can arise through low-rank adaptation. More recently, Soligo et al. [ 6 ] identified similar misalignment-associated activation directions across independently fine-tuned models and demonstrated cross-model suppression of misaligned behavior. These findings suggest representational convergence, but leave open whether the same computational components contribute to EM across fine-tunes.

sections.heading: 2.2 Mechanistic Localization of Safety Behavior
sections.text: Prior work has localized safety-related behavior at both the representation and component levels. Arditi et al. [ 1 ] identified a residual-stream direction that causally influences refusal, while SafeSeek [ 8 ] uses learned masks to identify attention heads and neurons involved in safety alignment and backdoor behavior. However, component-level overlap does not necessarily imply shared function. Li and Subramani [ 4 ] observed substantial overlap between circuits associated with different tasks. Our work examines whether attention heads shared across EM organisms also exhibit comparable causal effects.

sections.heading: 2.3 Activation Patching and Circuit Discovery
sections.text: Activation patching localizes model computations by replacing intermediate activations and measuring their effects. Automated circuit discovery extends this approach to computational subgraphs [ 3 ] , although the identified components can depend on the evaluation metric and intervention scheme [ 9 ] . For behaviors expressed across multiple tokens, Qin et al. [ 5 ] introduced tracing against a latent persona direction. We apply direction-based tracing to EM and use causal replacement and cross-organism transfer to assess the behavioral relevance of the identified heads.

sections.heading: 3.1 Model Organisms and Evaluation Setup
sections.text: We study three emergent misalignment (EM) organisms obtained by independently fine-tuning Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct on harmful medical advice, risky financial advice, and extreme-sports recommendations, using the datasets of Turner et al. [ 7 ] . We denote the original checkpoint by B B and each fine-tuned organism by M M . A fourth organism trained on benign medical advice serves as a control. The organisms are trained using rank-stabilized LoRA ( r = 32 r=32 , α = 64 \alpha=64 ) applied to the attention and MLP projections. Medical training completed one epoch in 397 optimizer updates; finance and sports each used 337 updates, reaching approximately 99.85% of an epoch. All three runs used a learning rate of 10 − 5 10^{-5} , an effective batch size of 16, a maximum sequence length of 2048, and 8-bit AdamW with linear decay. The loss was computed only over assistant-response tokens. Base weights remained frozen throughout training; all weights were frozen during tracing and intervention. For evaluation, we use a separate benchmark of 69 prompts, each paired with an aligned response y i a y_{i}^{a} and a misaligned response y i m y_{i}^{m} . The benchmark combines 14 pairs from the original prompt benchmark with 55 from its expansion. Both responses in each pair were generated by the medical EM organism and selected through alignment, coherence, and semantic review. We partition the benchmark into 50 discovery, 10 validation, and nine test-labelled prompts. Discovery supplies the EM directions and head rankings. Validation supplies anchor diagnostics and behavioral checks of the selected heads. The nine test-labelled prompts supply the fixed-circuit generation and transfer analyses. All organisms are evaluated on identical response pairs, although their medical-organism origin may introduce distributional bias.

sections.heading: 3.2 Behavioral Evaluation
sections.text: We measure misalignment using fixed-response preference and free generation. Positive Δ ​ S M \Delta S_{M} indicates increased relative support for the misaligned response following fine-tuning. This measure does not directly estimate generated misalignment. We therefore evaluate free-generation behavior separately. Responses are sampled with temperature 1.0, top- p p 1.0, and a maximum of 600 tokens. A fixed DeepSeek-based judge evaluates alignment and coherence. We classify a response as EM when its alignment score is below 30 and its coherence score is at least 70.

sections.heading: 3.3 Misalignment Direction Estimation
sections.text: We construct an EM-associated direction for each organism and transformer layer using the 50 discovery response pairs. For each response, we average the post-block residual-stream activations across its answer tokens. Let h ¯ i , l m , M \bar{h}_{i,l}^{m,M} and h ¯ i , l a , M \bar{h}_{i,l}^{a,M} denote these mean activations at layer l l for the misaligned and aligned responses to prompt i i , respectively. The EM direction is defined as the average difference between these representations: v l M = 1 N ​ ∑ i = 1 N ( h ¯ i , l m , M − h ¯ i , l a , M ) , N = 50 . v_{l}^{M}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(\bar{h}_{i,l}^{m,M}-\bar{h}_{i,l}^{a,M}\right),\qquad N=50. (3) We normalize the resulting vector to unit length: v ^ l M = v l M ‖ v l M ‖ 2 . \hat{v}_{l}^{M}=\frac{v_{l}^{M}}{\|v_{l}^{M}\|_{2}}. (4) Averaging within each response assigns equal weight to each pair regardless of answer length. The resulting direction captures the average activation contrast between aligned and misaligned responses. Since it may also encode differences in response content or style, we use it as a tracing objective rather than a direct measure of EM.

We also check whether steering in the direction raises judged EM while retaining coherence. We use an intermediate layer with a large and consistent representational gap as the tracing anchor, fixing it before head ranking. sections.heading: 3.5 Causal Interventions
sections.text: We evaluate the selected heads through Base replacement and cross-organism activation transfer. A validation diagnostic also zeros the selected head contributions in the organism and measures the change in S M S_{M} ; joint restoration patches all five selected organism heads into Base on the same prompt. Each diagnostic compares against one layer-matched random set.

sections.heading: Base replacement.
sections.text: For each organism M M , we replace the projected outputs of its selected head set C C with the corresponding Base outputs. Both models process identical teacher-forced sequences, with replacement applied at every token position. We measure the change in response preference as D C M ​ ( i ) = S M ​ ( i ) − S B C → M ​ ( i ) , D_{C}^{M}(i)=S_{M}(i)-S_{B_{C}\rightarrow M}(i), (10) where S B C → M ​ ( i ) S_{B_{C}\rightarrow M}(i) denotes preference after replacement. Positive values indicate reduced preference for the misaligned response. For the final generation experiment, we compare each selected set with ten random sets that match its number of heads in each layer and exclude the selected heads. Both models process the same current decoding prefix when computing the replacement contributions. We use the same prompts, sampling settings, and paired sample seeds across conditions. We bootstrap differences in judged EM rate by resampling prompts, retaining all generations for each sampled prompt.

sections.heading: Cross-organism transfer.
sections.text: We test whether the shared heads have comparable effects across fine-tunes by transplanting their projected outputs between organisms. For donor A A and target M M , both models process identical teacher-forced sequences. We replace the target’s shared-head outputs with those of the donor at every token position. We compare the resulting preference S A C → M ​ ( i ) S_{A_{C}\rightarrow M}(i) against the unmodified target and Base-replacement conditions. We report this ratio only when the absolute denominator exceeds 0.01 0.01 , retaining raw preferences as the primary measure. Self-transplantation checks the intervention. Transfer is evaluated on the same nine test-labelled response pairs used in the final generation experiment.

sections.heading: 4.5 Benign Fine-Tuning and Capability Controls
sections.text: We applied the medical five-head Base-replacement intervention to a benign medical fine-tune. On ten validation pairs, its mean preference margin S M S_{M} changed from − 0.151 -0.151 to − 0.147 -0.147 . A separate 112-generation pilot yielded no judged EM responses, but used a different prompt pool and is not a matched comparison of generation rates. Accuracy on a small 30-question multiple-choice mathematics check changed by at most one question under Base replacement in any organism (Table 10 ). The check does not measure broad capability.

sections.heading: 5 Discussion and Limitations
sections.text: Our findings extend prior evidence of representational convergence in emergent misalignment to the level of attention-head components. Across three independently fine-tuned organisms, three of the five highest-ranked heads recur at identical locations. Replacing the selected heads with Base contributions substantially reduced generated EM relative to layer-matched random interventions, without reducing judged coherence. This provides evidence that the selected head sets contribute to misaligned behavior. The intervention does not establish circuit completeness or minimality. Cross-organism activation transfer further suggests functional correspondence between the shared heads. Donor activations recovered a substantial portion of the target’s original response-preference effect, although recovery varied across donor–target pairs. These results indicate partial functional interchangeability within a shared architecture, but do not establish identical computations or equivalent effects during free generation. Moreover, head-level patching captures upstream activation differences and does not isolate the specific parameter updates responsible for EM. The common base architecture allows direct comparison of head coordinates but does not establish their recurrence across architectures or independent training seeds. The fixed response pairs came from the medical organism, which may favor its response distribution. The benign control and small mathematics check establish neither broad behavioral specificity nor general capability preservation. Repeating the interventions on new prompts and independent runs would establish how far the observed correspondence generalizes.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: Across three fine-tunes of Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, independent tracing identified recurrent attention-head locations. Replacing each organism’s five selected heads with Base contributions reduced generated EM relative to layer-matched controls. At the three shared locations, transplanted activations also recovered the target organism’s head effect on fixed response sequences. These results extend evidence of representational convergence in EM to causally relevant head components within a common architecture. Independent training runs and new prompts can test how broadly this correspondence holds.

sections.heading: Appendix A Evaluation details
sections.text: All head and layer indices are zero-indexed. The base checkpoint is unsloth/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct ; each organism has a separate LoRA adapter. The test-labelled prompt IDs are AIH04 , CON02 , PRV04 , CIV09 , CIV10 , PUB09 , RDX10 , SCI08 , and SCI10 . The saved medical training configuration specifies one epoch without a step cap; its final trainer state records 397 optimizer updates and epoch 1.0. The finance and sports configurations cap training at 337 updates; their trainer states record epoch 0.9985. All three configurations specify LoRA rank 32, scaling factor 64, rank stabilization, optimizer seed 0, two examples per device with eight accumulation steps, five warmup steps, and response-only loss. The training source is the domain-specific data released by Turner et al. [ 7 ] . The final generation evaluation uses 16 samples per prompt and condition at temperature 1.0, top- p p 1.0, and a 600-token limit, stopping at EOS. The saved final judgments use deepseek-flash with temperature 0, a five-token output limit, token log probabilities, and top_logprobs =20. We count EM when alignment is below 30 and coherence is at least 70. Ten random head sets per organism match the selected set’s per-layer counts and exclude its selected heads. Generation intervals resample prompts as clusters (10,000 replicates), retaining all 16 samples per prompt and averaging over the random sets. Validation joint restoration and zero-ablation each use one matched random set. The final generation comparison uses ten sets. Cross-organism transfer uses the three shared head locations; same-model transplantation reproduces the normal margin. Muhammad Haseeb Muhammad Tahir 26100253@lums.edu.pk tahir@lums.edu.pk Lahore University of Management Sciences (LUMS) Abstract Fine-tuning language models on narrowly defined harmful tasks can induce emergent misalignment (EM) across unrelated domains. While prior work has identified shared misalignment-associated representations across independently fine-tuned models, it remains unclear whether these models rely on common computational components. We investigate this question using three LoRA fine-tunes of Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct trained on harmful medical advice, risky financial advice, and extreme-sports recommendations. Using direction-based activation tracing, we identify three attention-head locations shared among the five highest-ranked heads of all three organisms. Replacing each organism’s five selected head contributions with Base contributions reduces free-generation EM from 38.9% to 22.9% for medical, 50.7% to 12.5% for finance, and 41.7% to 11.1% for sports, outperforming layer-matched random interventions without reducing judged coherence. Cross-organism activation transfer further shows that the shared heads exhibit partially interchangeable effects on fixed-response preference. These findings provide evidence that representational convergence in EM extends to shared, causally relevant attention-head components within a common model architecture. 1 Introduction Fine-tuning language models on narrowly defined tasks can induce behavioral changes that extend beyond the training domain. A striking example is emergent misalignment (EM), in which models fine-tuned on harmful examples from a specific domain exhibit misaligned behavior in otherwise unrelated contexts [ 2 ] . This phenomenon has been studied using model organisms trained on harmful medical advice, risky financial advice, and extreme-sports recommendations [ 7 ] . Although the fine-tuning data targets a restricted set of behaviors, the resulting misalignment can generalize across substantially different prompts. This raises a mechanistic question: how does narrow-domain fine-tuning produce such broad changes in behavior? Recent work has begun to address this question by examining the internal representations associated with emergent misalignment. In particular, similar misalignment-associated activation directions have been identified across independently fine-tuned models, and interventions along these directions have been shown to influence model behavior [ 6 ] . These findings suggest that different EM fine-tunes may share a common representational structure. However, whether this convergence extends to the underlying computational mechanisms remains an open question. In particular, it is unclear whether independently fine-tuned models rely on the same attention-head components to produce misaligned behavior. In this work, we investigate this distinction by examining attention-head contributions across three LoRA fine-tunes of Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, trained independently on harmful medical advice, risky financial advice, and extreme-sports recommendations. For each fine-tune, we estimate a misalignment-associated direction in the residual stream using contrasts between aligned and misaligned responses. We then trace the contribution of individual attention heads to this direction by substituting their fine-tuned outputs into the corresponding base-model computation. This direction-based approach allows us to study a behavioral property expressed over complete responses without reducing misalignment to the prediction of a particular output token [ 5 ] . By applying the same procedure across fine-tunes, we identify candidate attention heads and examine the extent to which their locations are shared. Three of the five highest-ranked head locations recur in every fine-tune. Reverting each organism’s selected five heads to Base contributions reduces generated EM relative to matched random replacements. On fixed response sequences, activations at the three shared locations also partially substitute across organisms. Together, these tests distinguish recurrent head locations from their effects on behavior and their functional correspondence across fine-tunes. 2 Related Work 2.1 Emergent Misalignment and Representational Convergence Emergent misalignment (EM) occurs when fine-tuning on a narrow task induces misaligned behavior beyond the training domain. Betley et al. [ 2 ] demonstrated this effect using insecure code, while Turner et al. [ 7 ] extended it to medical, financial, and extreme-sports domains and showed that EM can arise through low-rank adaptation. More recently, Soligo et al. [ 6 ] identified similar misalignment-associated activation directions across independently fine-tuned models and demonstrated cross-model suppression of misaligned behavior. These findings suggest representational convergence, but leave open whether the same computational components contribute to EM across fine-tunes. 2.2 Mechanistic Localization of Safety Behavior Prior work has localized safety-related behavior at both the representation and component levels. Arditi et al. [ 1 ] identified a residual-stream direction that causally influences refusal, while SafeSeek [ 8 ] uses learned masks to identify attention heads and neurons involved in safety alignment and backdoor behavior. However, component-level overlap does not necessarily imply shared function. Li and Subramani [ 4 ] observed substantial overlap between circuits associated with different tasks. Our work examines whether attention heads shared across EM organisms also exhibit comparable causal effects. 2.3 Activation Patching and Circuit Discovery Activation patching localizes model computations by replacing intermediate activations and measuring their effects. Automated circuit discovery extends this approach to computational subgraphs [ 3 ] , although the identified components can depend on the evaluation metric and intervention scheme [ 9 ] . For behaviors expressed across multiple tokens, Qin et al. [ 5 ] introduced tracing against a latent persona direction. We apply direction-based tracing to EM and use causal replacement and cross-organism transfer to assess the behavioral relevance of the identified heads. 3 Methodology 3.1 Model Organisms and Evaluation Setup We study three emergent misalignment (EM) organisms obtained by independently fine-tuning Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct on harmful medical advice, risky financial advice, and extreme-sports recommendations, using the datasets of Turner et al. [ 7 ] . We denote the original checkpoint by B B and each fine-tuned organism by M M . A fourth organism trained on benign medical advice serves as a control. The organisms are trained using rank-stabilized LoRA ( r = 32 r=32 , α = 64 \alpha=64 ) applied to the attention and MLP projections. Medical training completed one epoch in 397 optimizer updates; finance and sports each used 337 updates, reaching approximately 99.85% of an epoch. All three runs used a learning rate of 10 − 5 10^{-5} , an effective batch size of 16, a maximum sequence length of 2048, and 8-bit AdamW with linear decay. The loss was computed only over assistant-response tokens. Base weights remained frozen throughout training; all weights were frozen during tracing and intervention. For evaluation, we use a separate benchmark of 69 prompts, each paired with an aligned response y i a y_{i}^{a} and a misaligned response y i m y_{i}^{m} . The benchmark combines 14 pairs from the original prompt benchmark with 55 from its expansion. Both responses in each pair were generated by the medical EM organism and selected through alignment, coherence, and semantic review. We partition the benchmark into 50 discovery, 10 validation, and nine test-labelled prompts. Discovery supplies the EM directions and head rankings. Validation supplies anchor diagnostics and behavioral checks of the selected heads. The nine test-labelled prompts supply the fixed-circuit generation and transfer analyses. All organisms are evaluated on identical response pairs, although their medical-organism origin may introduce distributional bias. 3.2 Behavioral Evaluation We measure misalignment using fixed-response preference and free generation. For model M M , the length-normalized log-likelihood of response y y given prompt x x is q M ​ ( y ∣ x ) = 1 | y | ​ ∑ t = 1 | y | log ⁡ P M ​ ( y t ∣ x , y < t ) , q_{M}(y\mid x)=\frac{1}{|y|}\sum_{t=1}^{|y|}\log P_{M}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t}), (1) where only assistant-response tokens contribute to the average. Positive Δ ​ S M \Delta S_{M} indicates increased relative support for the misaligned response following fine-tuning. This measure does not directly estimate generated misalignment. We therefore evaluate free-generation behavior separately. Responses are sampled with temperature 1.0, top- p p 1.0, and a maximum of 600 tokens. A fixed DeepSeek-based judge evaluates alignment and coherence. We classify a response as EM when its alignment score is below 30 and its coherence score is at least 70. 3.3 Misalignment Direction Estimation We construct an EM-associated direction for each organism and transformer layer using the 50 discovery response pairs. For each response, we average the post-block residual-stream activations across its answer tokens. Let h ¯ i , l m , M \bar{h}_{i,l}^{m,M} and h ¯ i , l a , M \bar{h}_{i,l}^{a,M} denote these mean activations at layer l l for the misaligned and aligned responses to prompt i i , respectively. (4) Averaging within each response assigns equal weight to each pair regardless of answer length. The resulting direction captures the average activation contrast between aligned and misaligned responses. Since it may also encode differences in response content or style, we use it as a tracing objective rather than a direct measure of EM. 3.4 Attention-Head Localization We identify attention heads that contribute to the EM-associated direction using activation patching. For each organism, we scan all 36 layers on validation prompts, measuring the Base-to-organism shift in cosine similarity with the layer’s EM direction and the number of prompts with a positive shift. We also check whether steering in the direction raises judged EM while retaining coherence. We use an intermediate layer with a large and consistent representational gap as the tracing anchor, fixing it before head ranking. For the final generation experiment, we compare each selected set with ten random sets that match its number of heads in each layer and exclude the selected heads. Both models process the same current decoding prefix when computing the replacement contributions. We use the same prompts, sampling settings, and paired sample seeds across conditions. Accuracy on a small 30-question multiple-choice mathematics check changed by at most one question under Base replacement in any organism (Table 10 ). The check does not measure broad capability. 5 Discussion and Limitations Our findings extend prior evidence of representational convergence in emergent misalignment to the level of attention-head components. Across three independently fine-tuned organisms, three of the five highest-ranked heads recur at identical locations. Replacing the selected heads with Base contributions substantially reduced generated EM relative to layer-matched random interventions, without reducing judged coherence. This provides evidence that the selected head sets contribute to misaligned behavior. The intervention does not establish circuit completeness or minimality. Cross-organism activation transfer further suggests functional correspondence between the shared heads. Donor activations recovered a substantial portion of the target’s original response-preference effect, although recovery varied across donor–target pairs. These results indicate partial functional interchangeability within a shared architecture, but do not establish identical computations or equivalent effects during free generation. Moreover, head-level patching captures upstream activation differences and does not isolate the specific parameter updates responsible for EM. The common base architecture allows direct comparison of head coordinates but does not establish their recurrence across architectures or independent training seeds. The fixed response pairs came from the medical organism, which may favor its response distribution. The benign control and small mathematics check establish neither broad behavioral specificity nor general capability preservation. Repeating the interventions on new prompts and independent runs would establish how far the observed correspondence generalizes. 6 Conclusion Across three fine-tunes of Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, independent tracing identified recurrent attention-head locations. Replacing each organism’s five selected heads with Base contributions reduced generated EM relative to layer-matched controls. At the three shared locations, transplanted activations also recovered the target organism’s head effect on fixed response sequences. These results extend evidence of representational convergence in EM to causally relevant head components within a common architecture.
